newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan premier, foreign minister to visit Iran.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan premier, foreign minister to visit Iran.

text.p: Pakistani Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif will visit Tehran from June 16 to 17 for talks expected to focus on the conflict in neighbouring Afghanistan.

A Foreign Ministry official said Foreign Minister Gohar Ayub Khan was likely to pay a one-day visit to Tehran on June 13 and then accompany Sharif to the Iranian capital after the June 15 summit conference of the Developing-Eight (D-8) economic cooperation group of Islamic countries in Istanbul.
Relations between Iran and Pakistan, longstanding partners in the regional Economic Cooperation Organisation, have been strained by policy differences over Afghanistan.
Tehran and Islamabad both say they favour U.N. peace efforts aimed at formation of a broad-based Afghan government including all the ethnic, political and religious groups.
But Iran, deeply suspicious of the purist Islamic Taleban militia that has ruled Kabul since September, still recognises the ousted government of president Burhanuddin Rabbani.

Pakistan, which denies Afghan opposition charges that it supports the Taleban, became the first country formally to recognise the movement's government on May 25. Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates swiftly followed Islamabad's lead.
Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Viktor Pasouvaluk and Turkmenistan's Foreign Minister Boris Shikmuradov are both due in Islamabad on Saturday, with Afghanistan likely to be high on their agenda.

Iftikhar Murshid, additional secretary for Afghanistan at the Pakistani Foreign Ministry, said Turkmenistan's foreign minister had stated that he "fully understood and was supportive of Pakistan's position" on Afghanistan.

He said he had held talks earlier this week with Uzbek Foreign Minister Abdulaziz Komilov, who "told me that they (Uzbekistan) at first had reservations, but now he understands the reasons why we extended recognition".
Murshid said Pakistan had informed Iran, all the Central Asian States, Saudi Arabia and Russia before announcing its recognition of the Taleban administration in Kabul.
Iran, Russia and the Central Asian states have in the past expressed anxiety about the Taleban's religious militancy, which Tehran says has brought Islam into disrepute.
"We have tried to tell them (the Iranians), we have told everyone, including the Russians, that the way to bring about moderation is to engage with them (the Taleban)," Murshid said.
